analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock mining companies a reclamation fee to fund cleanup of thousands of abandoned mine sites polluting western streams.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either committee it was sent to, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a fee of 2% to 5% of net proceeds on companies producing gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals from public and formerly public lands, with the money going into a dedicated fund to clean up abandoned mines—sealing shafts, treating polluted drainage, and restoring damaged land and water. It would also let states, tribes, and other 'Good Samaritan' remediating parties get a federal water permit for cleanup work that shields them from enforcement liability, as long as they leave the water no worse than when they started. Today, cleanup is stalled because there is little dedicated funding and volunteers fear taking on liability for water discharges they didn't create.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and communities near thousands of abandoned hardrock mines in western states, whose public safety and water quality are threatened by mine drainage and runoff; states and tribes that would receive grants and annual inspections would improve cleanup oversight.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a dedicated, interest-bearing Abandoned Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund, financed by the new fee, that the Interior Secretary can spend without further appropriation to seal mine entries, treat polluted mine drainage, prevent erosion, and restore abandoned mine lands [S2][S3].

Spending is prioritized first on protecting the public from 'extreme danger' from past mining, then on restoring land, water, fish, and wildlife degraded by mining, with 25% of the money from each mine's fees spent back in the state where the mine is located [S3].

Creates a 'Good Samaritan' permit under the Clean Water Act so states, tribes, and other remediating parties can clean up abandoned mine sites without being treated as legally responsible for pre-existing pollution discharges, provided water quality is not made worse than the documented baseline [S2][S3].

Directs the EPA to provide public notice, comment, and hearing opportunities for each remediation permit application, and requires annual site inspections and periodic congressional reporting on every permit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies producing from unpatented claims or formerly patented federal mining claims, which would pay 2% to 5% of net proceeds into the cleanup fund; smaller operations with under $500,000 in annual proceeds from patented claims would be exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock gold and silver mining companies

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise the cost of producing gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals on federal lands, which supporters of the industry could argue pushes production and jobs overseas rather than reducing pollution [S3].

The Good Samaritan liability shield, while limited to remediating parties who leave water no worse than baseline, reduces the legal exposure of parties undertaking cleanup and could make some cleanups less thorough than full accountability would require [S3].
50% of the fund is distributed to states based on their share of national hardrock production from 1900 through 1980, a formula that may not match where cleanup needs are most urgent today [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed two real, documented obstacles—lack of cleanup money and fear of legal liability—that had stalled cleanup of thousands of abandoned mine sites damaging western streams [S3]. The fee falls directly on the industry that benefited from more than a century of mining under the 1872 law that left no reclamation requirement, and small operators are exempted. The main genuine trade-offs are the cost to domestic mineral producers and the fact that the liability shield makes cleanup less than perfect rather than legally watertight. On balance, it was a moderate, carefully scoped bill with real public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, split among two subcommittees, and the Interior Department was asked for its views, but neither committee ever scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Mark Udall introduced the bill on January 29, 2003, and 23 colleagues signed on as cosponsors, 21 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S1][S4].
The Speaker referred it to both the Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on January 29, 2003 [S1][S5].

Within weeks it was routed to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee (January 30) and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee (February 12), and the Interior Department was asked for its comments [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, in either the House or the Senate, through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies avoided a 2-5% reclamation fee on production from federal lands, while communities living with abandoned mine hazards and polluted streams gained no new cleanup funding or liability relief. Taxpayers continue to bear the open-ended exposure for sites where no responsible party can pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies, which avoided the fee

for.name: Rep. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Abandoned Hardrock Mines Reclamation Act and delivered introductory remarks on it twice in early 2003.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors (21 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referring the bill to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever held during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referring the bill to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: The industry that would pay the new reclamation fee
against.what_they_did: The organized mining industry has historically opposed mandatory reclamation fees on hardrock production from federal lands, which had failed repeatedly in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the 23 cosponsors were bipartisan (21 Democrats, 2 Republicans), and no recorded opposition ever surfaced.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and similar minerals on federal lands)
industries.note: The bill would charge companies 2% to 5% of net proceeds from mines on unpatented and formerly patented federal claims to fund cleanup of abandoned mine sites—a direct cost to current producers for a public harm the industry's operations created over more than a century under the fee-free 1872 Mining Law. Small operators under $500,000 in annual proceeds are exempt [S3].

industries.industry: Environmental remediation, water treatment and engineering firms
industries.note: The bill would channel reclamation fund grants and Good Samaritan permit work to parties conducting mine cleanups, creating demand for site assessment, drainage treatment, and long-term monitoring work at abandoned mine sites [S2][S3].

industries.industry: State and tribal governments in mining states
industries.note: States and tribes would gain new cleanup grants, delegated permitting authority, and a liability shield for Good Samaritan projects, but they must first complete statewide abandoned mine inventories and run approved reclamation programs to receive the money [S3].
